topic: Tarique Rahman Becomes Bangladesh's Next PM

subtopics.title: Tarique Rahman's Rise and Oath
subtopics.summary: Tarique Rahman emerged as the top leader of the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) and assumed office as Prime Minister of Bangladesh. He returned to Bangladesh after 17 years and took the oath at Parliament South Plaza in Dhaka. His government succeeded the overthrown government of Sheikh Hasina after 18 months of upheaval.

subtopics.title: 2026 Election Results and Parliament
subtopics.summary: The BNP, led by Tarique Rahman, won the 13th General Election with 209 seats, an absolute majority, ending the Awami League's two-decade dominance. Jamaat-e-Islami emerged as the second-largest party with 68 seats. Bangladesh's legislature is unicameral, with 300 members elected directly and 50 seats reserved for women and allocated proportionally among parties.

subtopics.title: Political Background and Transitions
subtopics.summary: Bangladesh became independent from Pakistan in 1971, and Sheikh Mujibur Rahman became Prime Minister in 1972. Power then passed through Ziaur Rahman, Khaleda Zia and Sheikh Hasina, and the BNP last governed in 2001-2006. The 2024-2026 interim period followed a student-led revolution and Hasina's flight to India.

subtopics.title: July National Charter and PM Power Limits
subtopics.summary: The July National Charter (Constitutional Amendment) Implementation Order 2025 is a 28-page reform agreement signed by 25 political parties and the interim government led by Muhammad Yunus. It secured 65.3% yes votes in a referendum. It caps a PM's lifetime service at 10 years, bars the PM from holding both party and government head roles, and creates a two-house parliament.

subtopics.title: India-Bangladesh Ties Under the New Government
subtopics.summary: Ties between India and Bangladesh moved from strained relations in 2001-2006 to a 'Golden Chapter' under Sheikh Hasina from 2009 to 2024. quizzes.passage:
Bangladesh entered a new political phase in February 2026. The Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), led by Tarique Rahman, won the 13th General Election and ended the Awami League's long dominance in the country. The result came after roughly eighteen months of upheaval and marked a major political shift. The BNP has a long history in Bangladesh's politics, and its win gave it an absolute majority in the legislature.

Tarique Rahman succeeded the government of Sheikh Hasina, which had been overthrown. He had come back to Bangladesh before taking up the highest office, and he is now the country's Prime Minister. He took the oath of office at Parliament South Plaza in Dhaka, and Om Birla attended the swearing-in ceremony.

His rise marks the emergence of a new top leader for the BNP. The party's leadership now faces the task of governing a country that has been through a period of political instability. The change follows a student-led revolution and Hasina's flight to India, which left the country in a period of political uncertainty. The election result and the swearing-in have drawn attention both inside Bangladesh and across the region. The booklet presents this as a major turning point in the country's current affairs.

quizzes.passage:
Bangladesh's interim government, led by Muhammad Yunus, took part in a major constitutional reform agreement known as the July National Charter. The agreement aims to build what is described as the country's Second Republic and to prevent future authoritarianism. It was signed by a group of political parties together with the interim government, and the reforms were then put to voters in a referendum.

The charter places new limits on the Prime Minister. A lifetime term limit will apply to any individual serving as PM, and the Prime Minister will no longer be able to serve as head of the party and head of government at the same time. The PM also cannot declare a state of emergency alone, because the decision needs written consent from the cabinet and the leader of the opposition.

The charter also changes Parliament. The existing Jatiya Sangsad will become the Lower House, and a new Upper House, called the Senate, will be created. Reserved seats for women in the Lower House will be increased. The Deputy Speaker must be elected from the main opposition party, and a controversial rule that removes MPs who vote against their party will be removed or weakened.

Other changes cover elections and institutions. A non-partisan caretaker government will oversee general elections, and paper ballots will be mandatory. A Supreme Judicial Council and an independent Judicial Appointments Commission are to be formed. Several commissions will receive full financial and administrative independence.
